text: This is the last lesson of the entire ServiceNow Administrator to Developer to Technical Architect path. Fourteen courses, and it's worth walking back through what they actually built, rather than letting them blur into one long list.

Course 1 gave you the ITSM and ITIL 4 foundations underneath everything else. Courses 2 and 3 gave you base platform literacy. Course 4 made you fluent in Flow Designer automation. Courses 5 and 6 took you into real server-side development — Business Rules, Script Includes, a genuine scoped application. Course 7 connected the platform to the outside world through integrations. Course 8 put those ITSM foundations into real configured practice, and Course 9 took on configuration-item data modeling, one of the platform's genuinely hardest, most overlooked skills.

Courses 10 through 13 rounded out what a production instance depends on day to day — access control design, a real application lifecycle, diagnostic instincts under load, and enterprise-scale architecture judgment. And this course closed the loop with the Meridian Health Network capstone: requirements actually gathered, workflows and integrations actually built, test plans actually run, documentation actually produced, and architecture decisions actually presented and defended under real follow-up questions. That's your proof, not a claim — built honestly on a Personal Developer Instance, exactly the way Lesson 9 described, and genuinely demonstrable in front of a real interviewer.

Finishing this path is a real milestone, not a finish line. ServiceNow keeps shipping new platform releases on its own cycle, and staying current with what changes is an ongoing professional habit now. Chapter 1 laid out the CIS specialization landscape honestly — this path built genuine depth in CIS-ITSM and CIS-Discovery specifically, and choosing one of those, or another with eyes open, is a real next step. And Chapter 2, Lesson 7 was direct about this: real experience across multiple real engagements, not another certification, is the actual path toward Technical Architect candidacy.

You started this path somewhere short of knowing what ServiceNow even was as a platform. You're finishing it having planned certification pathways, understood the real job market, built a genuine portfolio, and completed a full enterprise capstone project you can describe, show, and defend by name — the Meridian Health Network consolidation, built with your own hands across these last two courses. That is real, earned progress, fourteen courses' worth of it. Take the portfolio, the resume, and that capstone story out into real interviews. Stay current with the platform, consider a CIS specialization built on the real depth you already have, and let real project experience keep building toward whatever comes next, Technical Architect candidacy included, one real decision at a time. Congratulations on finishing the whole path — now go get the job.
